claims.claim: Amphilochius of Iconium was a Christian bishop of the fourth century, born perhaps at Caesarea around 339/340 and died probably between 394 and 403.
Amphilochius was bishop of the important see of Iconium, probably placed there by Basil of Caesarea early in 374.
Amphilochius was probably first cousin to Gregory of Nazianzus and was brought up in the Christian aristocracy of Cappadocia.
He studied law in Antioch with Libanius and practised at Constantinople before retiring to lead a religious life.
The work In mulierem peccatricem is a homily by Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, on the sinful woman who anointed the Lord with myrrh and on the Pharisee.
In mulierem peccatricem is also known as Homily IV among Amphilochius's surviving works.

The homily is marked by an almost excessive use of imagery taken from both Scripture and contemporary life, which serves as a constant binding or structural element in the development and forward movement of the narrative.

Amphilochius's homiletic style in this work can be defined as one of descriptive and dramatic representation of biblical episodes, using imagery to establish a picturesque world in which biblical characters move and act and to involve the audience.
The work survives in Greek manuscript tradition and is listed as CPG 3234 in the Clavis Patrum Graecorum.
The date of the author is given as approximately 3rd to 4th century CE or A.D. 4 in the Thesaurus Linguae Graecae canon.

Amphilochius was very energetic against the Messalians and contributed to the extirpation of that group, and he also fought against Arianism and defended the divinity of the Holy Spirit against the Macedonians.
